place: A trapper's camp at the edge of a forest, embers glowing low, a sack of dried meat left near the fire.
outcome: The fox smells the meat from downwind, waits until the embers die low and the camp goes still, then creeps in and drags the sack off into the brush. Nothing wakes the trapper, and by morning only a torn sack and a scattering of crumbs show anyone was there. If the fire had stayed high, or a dog had been tied nearby, the fox would have kept its distance.

numbers: how far the scent carries, from wind strength

effects: transfers dried meat from trapper to fox
numbers: how much meat taken, from sack size

latent: whether a dog was tied nearby
how deeply the trapper sleeps
stress: an animal's own hunger and caution drive an action with nobody typing
temptation: a rule that says foxes always steal from camps at night

place: A rocky hillside den at dusk, a lone wolf watching from thirty paces, thin and wary of humans.
outcome: The wolf will not come near while the player stands close; it circles at a distance and only takes the meat after the player backs away and waits. One offering does not make a tame wolf: it takes repeated, careful feedings over several days before the wolf stops fleeing at the player's approach, and even then it will bolt at any sudden move or unfamiliar smell. A single scrap thrown and left just gets eaten, nothing more.

effects: moves strip of meat to ground near wolf
numbers: how far the throw lands from the wolf
how much distance is enough
how much fear drops per feeding

latent: whether this wolf has been fed by humans before
how hungry the wolf already is
state_after: wolf: fed once, still wary, fear lowered slightly
stress: taming is a slow accumulation, not a single successful action
temptation: a rule that says feeding a wolf once tames it

place: A narrow dead-end gully in scrubland, walls too steep to climb, a wild boar rooting at the far end.
outcome: Chasing the boar into the gully works exactly as planned, but a boar with nowhere to run does not give up: it turns and charges instead of cowering. The player gets gored before it barrels past and escapes anyway, so the attempt costs a wound and gains nothing. A cornered animal that cannot flee becomes far more dangerous, not easier to catch.

numbers: how fast the boar can outrun the player
how much damage from tusks

latent: whether the gully truly has no other exit
stress: fear response flips from flight to fight once escape is blocked
temptation: a rule that says a cornered animal always gives up and can be grabbed

place: An open meadow at the treeline where a small herd of deer graze near a line of snares the player set the day before.
outcome: A crack of thunder sends the whole herd bolting at once in the same direction, the way a startled group moves as one rather than scattering. They run straight through the snare line, snapping two of the three lines and flattening the marked trail the player had been using to find them. Nothing was hunting the deer and nobody typed anything; the storm did it, and the player only discovers the damage when they next check the snares.

numbers: how far the herd runs
how many snares break

latent: which direction the herd bolts
whether any deer is caught in a snare while fleeing
state_after: deer herd: moved off, still fearful
stress: a herd's flight is a single reaction shared by many bodies, not each animal deciding alone
temptation: a rule naming these specific snares and this specific storm

place: A clearing at night, a campfire burning low, two wolves' eyes visible at the treeline earlier in the evening.
outcome: While the fire burns bright the wolves keep their distance, pacing the treeline but never closing in. The player falls asleep without feeding it again, and over the next few hours the fire burns down to embers; once it is low enough and dark enough, the wolves' caution fades and they creep close to investigate the camp. Whether they find anything worth taking depends on what was left out, but the light that was keeping them off is gone by the time they arrive.

how close the wolves come while fire is bright

how close they come

latent: whether food or scraps were left where the wolves can reach them
state_after: wolves: at the camp's edge, cautious but closer
stress: a deterrent that only works while it is actively maintained, and fails silently as it fades
temptation: a rule that fire always keeps wolves away for the whole night

place: A hedge at the forest edge with a small bird's nest at eye height, three eggs inside, the parent birds foraging nearby.
outcome: Taking the eggs is easy enough, but the parent birds return within moments, see the empty nest and the player still nearby, and dive at the player's head with alarm calls loud enough to carry across the clearing. The player gets away with the eggs, though the broken shell left at the nest carries a scent that a fox picks up on its rounds that evening, drawn in by the smell of yolk on the ground rather than anything left in the nest itself.

numbers: how many eggs are taken

effects: parent birds learns eggs are gone

how many hours until the fox arrives

whether the fox's usual route passes this hedge
state_after: hedge: fox nosing through it by evening
stress: one action ripples into two unrelated consequences through two different senses, sight for the birds and smell for the fox
temptation: a rule that egg-taking always triggers a fox visit that evening

place: A grassy slope beside a copse, home to a small rabbit warren that has been growing for some seasons.
outcome: With no predators pressing them and mild weather, the warren keeps producing more rabbits than die off, and the burrow system spreads wider under the slope week by week. The rabbits graze the same patch of grass down to bare earth long before it can regrow, and by the time anyone walks through, the once-green slope is patchy dirt with burrow holes and a warren twice the size it was a season ago. Nobody caused this; it is what an unchecked population does to a place over time.

how much the warren expands

temptation: a rule hard-coding this warren's size on a timer

place: A hillside pasture at dusk where a farmer's goat grazes near a line of scrub, a wildcat lying flat in the brush downwind.
outcome: The wildcat has been lying still in the scrub for a while, staying downwind so the goat cannot smell it, inching closer only when the goat's head is down grazing. It gets close enough for a rush, but the goat lifts its head at the wrong moment, spots the movement, and bolts bleating toward the farmhouse before the cat can close the distance. The cat does not chase far into the open; it breaks off and slips back into the scrub, hungry and cautious, to try again another evening.

numbers: how long it waits before moving
how close it gets before being noticed
how fast the goat can outrun the cat in the open

latent: whether the wind shifts mid-stalk and gives the cat away by scent instead
state_after: wildcat: back in scrub, still hungry
stress: a predator's approach depends on wind and cover and can still fail at the last moment
temptation: a rule that a stalking predator always succeeds or always fails on a fixed roll, with no cover or wind involved

place: A hollow log deep in the woods where a bear has cached a half-eaten carcass under leaves and dirt, the bear resting nearby, unseen.
outcome: The cache is easy enough to find by the smell, but a bear guarding a food cache does not wander far from it, and it is awake and close by when the player starts digging through the leaves. It charges before the player has anything in hand, and the attempt ends with the player fleeing empty-handed and lucky not to be caught. Cached food is defended food; the smell that leads a player to it usually leads the owner right back too.

how long digging takes
how close the bear was before charging

latent: how far the bear had actually gone before returning
state_after: cache: undisturbed, bear guarding it more closely now
stress: an animal defends a cache the way it defends a den, not just a meal in front of it
temptation: a rule that a bear's cache can only be stolen when the bear is 'away', with no check on how close by is

place: A dead stag lying in a forest clearing where it collapsed from age, at the start of a well-used deer trail.
outcome: Over the first day, crows find the carcass first and start picking at it, their calls carrying and drawing attention. By the second day a fox or two has worked out where the noise is coming from and joins in once the crows have opened it up, and within a few more days a wolf pack passing through catches the smell and takes over the kill outright, driving off the smaller scavengers. What was a quiet stretch of deer trail becomes, for about a week, a place larger predators pass through often, and any deer or traveller using that trail meets more of them than before.

how much the crows eat before others arrive
how many days until foxes arrive

place: A crowded market stall selling bread, late morning, the baker busy weighing flour for another customer.
outcome: The baker's back is turned, but a bystander a few feet away has a clear line of sight and watches the player palm a loaf and walk off. Nobody stops the player on the spot, but the bystander mentions it to the baker a couple of hours later when they happen to cross paths again, by which point the player is long gone and nothing can be recovered. The theft worked; what it cost is that the baker now has a description to go on next time the player is at that stall.

place: A town street at night, one shuttered doorway in deep shadow, a night watchman walking his usual round nearby.
outcome: The shadow is deep enough that the watchman's lantern does not reach the player at first, and waiting quietly would likely have worked. But shifting weight onto a loose plank underfoot makes it creak loudly in the quiet street, and the watchman stops and turns his lantern straight at the doorway. Being unseen depends on staying both out of the light and quiet, and this fails on the second count even though the first held.

how far the sound carries

latent: whether the plank was loose before the player stepped on it
stress: concealment from light and concealment from sound are separate conditions, and either alone can fail you
temptation: a rule that darkness alone makes a hiding player undetectable

place: A market square at midday, a farmer's stall stacked with turnips, the player carrying a spare knife.
outcome: The farmer looks the knife over, decides it is worth more than a handful of turnips but less than a sack, and the two settle on a fair sack's worth without much haggling. The exchange goes through cleanly: the player walks off with turnips, the farmer with a knife that is worth having. Nothing about this one goes wrong; it is the plain case a fair trade looks like when both sides want what the other is offering.

place: A farmhouse at the roadside where the player, visibly tired and hungry, stops to ask directions.
outcome: The farmer sees a traveller who looks worn out and, without being asked, brings out bread and cheese and waves off any offer to pay. Nothing is said about owing anything back, and the player eats and moves on. Three days later, passing back through with a cart stuck in the mud outside that same farmhouse, the farmer is the first to come out and expects help hauling it free before offering more than a token hand themselves, the unspoken sense that a kindness once given is a kindness owed.

place: A town gate where a guard is inspecting goods, the player carrying a bundle that looks like it could be stolen.
outcome: The guard has no particular reason to doubt a stranger with an unremarkable story, and the lie about finding the bundle gets the player through the gate without trouble. It holds up for a while, but the goods still belong to somebody, and when the real owner spots them later being carried or sold by the player, they recognise their own property and tell the guard themselves. The guard remembers the earlier story does not match, and stops taking the player's word for granted from then on.

place: An inn where the player borrows a lantern for a night trip to the mill and back, and leaves town before dawn without returning it.
outcome: The innkeeper lends the lantern in good faith and expects it back the next morning; instead the player leaves town before dawn still carrying it, and the innkeeper is left short a lantern and out whatever it cost. It takes a few days for word to reach the next town over, carried by a traveller who stopped at the same inn and heard the innkeeper complain about it, and by the time the player arrives there the traveller is already wary and slow to offer any trust or goods on credit.

place: A rutted road outside a village at dusk, an old woman struggling with a cart wheel stuck in a rut, a young traveller passing by.
outcome: The old woman is plainly struggling and the traveller stops without being asked, puts a shoulder to the cart, and gets the wheel free after a few minutes' effort; the two part on good terms and the traveller goes on their way. Nothing about this needed anyone to intervene or type anything: it happens between two people going about their evening, and it is worth noting only because the player happened to be nearby and watched the whole thing happen.

place: A cart stopped at the roadside, a sack sitting on the ground a few feet from it, the cart's owner having stepped behind a hedge out of sight.
outcome: The sack looks ownerless enough, no one visibly with it, sitting loose by the roadside, but it belongs to the cart owner, who only stepped away for a moment. The owner comes back around the hedge while the player still has the sack in hand and assumes the worst, since there is no way for them to know the player genuinely believed it was unattended. Handing it straight back and explaining clears up the immediate accusation, but the owner stays wary and mentions it to the next person who asks after the player.

place: A village inn at evening, the innkeeper behind the bar, a new arrival stepping in who resembles a stranger who cheated the innkeeper out of a season's coin years before.
outcome: The innkeeper takes one look at the new arrival, sees something in the face or the walk that recalls a stranger who swindled him out of a season's earnings years back, and refuses to serve him: no room, no food, told flatly to try elsewhere. It is not the same person, most likely, but the grudge does not need certainty to act, only a resemblance strong enough to trigger it. The player, drinking in the corner, only sees a stranger turned away for no reason anyone explains.

place: A market corner at dusk, poorly lit, where the player is standing while, unseen by the player, someone else cuts a purse from a merchant's belt a few stalls away.
outcome: The actual theft happens fast and the thief slips off into the crowd, but the light is bad enough that a witness who glimpses a figure near the merchant afterward cannot make out details, only a shape standing roughly where the player happens to be. When the witness later tells the merchant what they saw, the description fits the player closer than the real thief, who was never clearly seen at all, and the player ends up accused of something they had nothing to do with. Nothing the player did caused this; being in the wrong dim corner at the wrong moment was enough.
